text.p: (Compiled for Reuters by Media Monitors)
THE AUSTRALIAN FINANCIAL REVIEW

Yesterday, the leader of the government in the Senate, Robert Hill, revealed the Federal Government may reject the Productivity Commission's call to cut car industry tariffs to five per cent by 2000, saying Cabinet decisions would not be made on ideological gronds and the Government is determined to ensure Australia develops viable manufacturing industries. Page 1.

While many resort owners are currently struggling to make ends meet in underperforming resort properties, the theme park industry is so strong at the moment that operators in the Brisbane-Gold Coast area, where most of the country's parks are concentrated, are planning about $300 million in new development this calendar year. Page 1.

After an agreement with British Airports Authority, AMP has 'Australianised' its consortium bid for Melbourne's Tullamarine Airport, as BAA cuts its stake in return for an AMP agreement to cut its equity in any future joint bids for foreign airport sites. The shake-up came as the Federal Government closed bidding yesterday. Page 3.

Aboriginal activist Noel Pearson yesterday said the Federal Government's rejection of a human rights clause in a trade treaty with Europe indicated it was preparing to set aside the Racial Discrimination Act following the controversial Wik High Court ruling. A spokesman for Prime Minister John Howard however, said the decision had nothing to do with native title, and was decided upon months before the Wik decision. Page 3.
THE AUSTRALIAN

The results of the West inquiry into higher education, which is due to report later this year, already indicate a grim feeling within Australia's universities. Academics surveyed said the future of higher education is "dismal" and they would not recommend an academic career to anyone. Page 1

A senior Federal Government Minister, Senator Robert Hill, has broken ranks and challenged the push for rapid cuts to car industry protection as a row broke out between the Governments of Queensland and car manufacturing states Victoria and South Australi over tariff levels in the industry. Page 1

Australia's largest health insurance fund, Medibank Private, is pushing to limit the amount it pays private hospitals for its members in a move hospitals and doctors believe will force services to be rationed and create waiting lists for private hospital treatment. Medibank has introduced the move into contracts currently under negotiation with 10 Victorian hospitals. Page 1.

Three unions face the first Federal Court injunctions under the tough new Workplace Relations Act after petroleum group Mobil moved to end an industrial dispute at its Victorian operations. Mobil has made the court applications, which will effectively ban all industrial action for the next six months. If the injunction is granted unions could face fines if the action continues. Page 2.
THE SYDNEY MORNING HERALD

The Australian Tax Office has declared war on tax cheats with the establishment of a task force to target allegations of a rampant cash economy. The ATO believes there is widespread cheating amongst small business and plans to introduce new measures to raise the level of income reporting. Page 1

The Australian Broadcasting Authority has released a report advocating the introduction of digital terrestrial television as early as possible. The new technology will offer clearer signals, improved quality and choice, but will also involve millions of dollars of investment by networks and consumers to upgrade technology. Page 1.

Federal Environment Minister Senator Robert Hill will next week push to change the Great Barrier Reef's legislation, allowing Australian and foreign warships to discharge waste into the World Heritage-listed marine park. The amendment is designed to allow navy vessels to discharge waste during a joint US-Australian military exercise to be held later this year. Page 3.

New South Wales Police Commissioner Peter Ryan has been praised by a former commissioner for "having the guts" to carry out controversial reforms in the force. John Avery said some of the senior police officers removed by Ryan early this week were "good cops" but the size of the hierarchy had to be reduced. Page 2.
THE AGE

Communications Minister Richard Alston is set to beef up the anti-siphoning laws, introduced to prevent the slide of major sporting events to pay-TV, after efforts to have the Australian cricket tour of South Africa shown live on free-to-air television mised the mark. Channel Seven has the free-to-air rights to cover the three Tests and seven one-day internationals, but has only scheduled one-hour highlight shows, revealing that it did not have any rights for live telecasts. Page 1.

Environment Minister Robert Hill yesterday indicated the Federal Government would reject Productivity Commission proposals to scrap most or all assistance to the car industry. This indication came as Victorian Premier Jeff Kennett and Southcorp managing irector Graeme Kraehe accused the Government of lacking an industry policy to encourage investment in Australia. Page 1.

Labor said yesterday the Australian economy could cope with a safety net wage increase of at least A$14 a week after this week's low inflation forecasts, and while the Democrats agree, Industrial Relations Minister Peter Reith has stood by the Government's original A$8-a-week offer saying anything more could blow those inflation prospects. Page 2.

The Australian Health Insurance Association yesterday told a Productivity Commission inquiry into private health insurance that funds should follow the US system of managed care, where the fund itself dictates a patients treatment and its cost. Medical and hospital organisationsn howevern have raised concerns over the private insurance industry's bid to introduce this system, and to take charge of their consumers Medicare levy payments. Page 2.
